audit_notes: Model: steady advection-diffusion of absorbing dirt in a surface layer that recedes at the photo-chalking velocity v = photon flux x quantum yield x molar volume / (N_A x co-binder fraction); surface deposition minus wash-off; clean deep boundary; the areal dirt load is transformed into the daily-mean roof heat flux (same sol-air model as the other roof concepts). Adjustment: with the proposed quantum yield 1e-5 the formula gives 18 um/yr, about twice the chalking rates measured for anatase-pigmented paints in Florida/Arizona (5-10 um/yr); I calibrate the effective quantum yield to 5e-6 (v = 2.8e-13 m/s, ~9 um/yr), so 0.5 mm lasts ~55 years. Baseline: durable acrylic cool coating with 50 % binder and effective yield 2.8e-6, giving the 0.5 um/yr erosion used before; k_abs = 316 m2/kg is calibrated to the CRRC-type baseline loss 0.85 -> 0.67. Hand result: design m = 2e-11*5e-6/(2.8e-13 + 1.6e-13) = 2.3e-4 kg/m2 -> dAlpha 0.072 -> SR 0.83 -> q = 0.5*(0.172*300 + 150 - 0.92*85)/15.5 = 3.97 W/m2 vs 5.56 W/m2: ~-29 %. Caveats: the erosion rate is now tied to the UV dose, which varies only ~+-30 % among hot climates, but the quantum yield is uncertain by a factor ~5 and the removal of loose chalk still needs wind or rain (in calm, dry periods chalk and dirt stay, although chalk is itself white); the extra benefit of anatase oxidising organic soot is not modelled; the gain still follows largely from the ratio of erosion velocities. Structural: chalky top layer has low cohesion (rubs off, stains), the silicate matrix below is sound; anatase photocatalysis degrades adjacent sealants and organic roof membranes at the edges. Simulation coefficient: effective dirt removal velocity v + k_w = 4.4e-13 m/s.
